title: A Demonstration of Correlation Analysis in Python & Quarto using Planets
text:
Introduction

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set_context('talk')

df = sns.load_dataset('planets')
df = df[['orbital_period', 'mass']].dropna()
df.shape[0]

513


Does a planet’s orbital period correlate with its mass?
The students of the UW-Madison DSHB program are interested in learning about correlations between planetary orbital periods and planetary masses. This project uses the Seaborn planets dataset to demonstrate correlation analysis in Python and Quarto. After removing observations with missing values in either variable, we have 513 planets available for analysis.


Lit Review


Methods
We have two continuous numerical variables: orbital period, measured in days, and planetary mass, measured in Jupiter masses. We will evaluate their linear association using Pearson correlation and a scatterplot. Because these variables can be highly skewed, the results should be interpreted cautiously.


Results

corr_val = df['orbital_period'].corr(df['mass'])

if corr_val > 0.8:
    narrative = "a very strong positive correlation"
elif corr_val > 0.4:
    narrative = "a moderate positive correlation"
elif corr_val > 0:
    narrative = "a positive but weak correlation"
elif corr_val > -0.4:
    narrative = "a moderate negative correlation"
elif corr_val > -0.8:
    narrative = "a moderate negative correlation"
else:
    narrative = "a very strong negative correlation"

Using the simple Pearson correlation approach, these data produce a correlation coefficient of 0.17373. We conclude the relationship is a positive but weak correlation.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))

sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='orbital_period', y='mass', ax=ax)

ax.set_xlabel('Orbital Period (days)')
ax.set_ylabel('Planetary Mass (Jupiter masses)')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
